title: Frances of Rome (9 March)
hook: a wife and mother in Rome who cared for the sick in plague years

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of God, the bookseller locked up as mad who came out to care for the sick. Your line was the hospitaller. Who did you call or visit? Day nine hundred seventy-four.

A woman sits down with her prayer book in a big Roman house. She opens to the psalm for the hour and reads the first line. Someone calls her: a servant with a question. She marks the place, goes, comes back, reads the same line. Her husband needs her. She goes again. Then a child. Then a guest. Tradition says she was called away from that one verse again and again, and every time she went without complaint. When she finally came back for good, the story goes, the verse on the page was written in gold. Today is about Frances of Rome.
screen: `ONE VERSE, STARTED AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `CALLED AWAY, AND GOING.` → `THE VERSE IN GOLD.`

segments.voice: Frances, tradition says, wanted from girlhood to enter a convent. Her family arranged a marriage instead, to a young nobleman named Lorenzo Ponziani. She was miserable at first. Then, with her sister-in-law Vannozza, she found her way: the two of them, in their fine clothes, slipping out to visit the sick and the poor of the city. The marriage became a long and loving one, and she raised her children in it. Then came hard years for Rome: war, famine and plague. Frances turned the family house into a place of care. She gave away the household's grain and wine, nursed the sick, and, tradition says, buried one of her own children in the plague. She was a mother in mourning, and still out in the streets. There's a saying handed down from her that sums her up, often put this way: a married woman must sometimes leave God at the altar to find him in her housekeeping. That's the gold verse, in a sentence. Prayer was never less important to her. Serving was simply prayer by other means. In the Douay-Rheims, the book of Proverbs describes a valiant woman: "She hath opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her hands to the poor." Later, Frances gathered a group of women who lived that way, without taking full vows, and after her husband died she joined them. Tradition also says she saw her guardian angel at her side, lighting her way at night, which is why she's a patron of drivers. Her holiness ran through the house, not around it.
screen: `SHE WANTED THE CONVENT, AND GOT A MARRIAGE.` · `PLAGUE YEARS: THE HOUSE BECOMES CARE.` · `LEAVE GOD AT THE ALTAR, FIND HIM AT HOME.` · `AN ANGEL TO LIGHT THE WAY.` · then, large: `SHE HATH OPENED HER HAND TO THE NEEDY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for someone at home. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people under your roof, or the ones you'd call home if you live alone: a partner, a child, a parent, a roommate, a neighbor down the hall. Find one small need of theirs you've been stepping around. A dish, a question, a cup of tea, a few minutes of listening. Picture yourself putting down whatever you're in the middle of and going to them, the way Frances closed the book. If you pray, you can offer that small errand as your prayer. If you don't, just breathe, and get ready to go. The bell holds the time.
Frances of Rome. A Roman wife and mother who nursed the sick in plague years and left her prayers, again and again, to serve.
Your line: she left prayer to serve. Today, when someone interrupts you, try treating the interruption as the point. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholics keep 9 March as the optional memorial of Saint Frances of Rome; in Rome her body is venerated at the church of Santa Francesca Romana in the Forum, and in some places cars are blessed on her feast because she is patron of drivers.
